title: Registry of an Integrated Longitudinal Multimodal Biospecimen Biobank for Primary CNS Lymphoma in China
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] This project aims to establish and prospectively register a longitudinal, multimodal biobank for primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL). The study will primarily enroll patients undergoing needle biopsy or surgical resection of lesions involving the brain, spinal cord, or meninges, with a pathological diagnosis of central nervous system lymphoma. To ensure population homogeneity, patients with PCNSL will constitute the core analysis cohort. Patients with imaging findings suggestive of PCNSL but a final pathological diagnosis other than PCNSL will serve as disease controls, and matched healthy volunteers will be recruited as baseline controls. At baseline, biopsy tissue, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), peripheral blood, urine, saliva, and stool samples will be collected. Follow-up visits will be scheduled at 1 month after biopsy and every 3-6 months thereafter, with contrast-enhanced brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and serial collection of CSF and peripheral blood. After the requirements of routine pathological diagnosis have been met, biopsy specimens will undergo tiered multi-omics profiling according to sample availability and freshness, including whole-exome sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing, metabolomics, spatial transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics. Analyses of CSF and blood samples will focus on circulating tumor DNA and cell-free RNA (ctDNA/cfRNA), supplemented by conventional cytology, flow cytometry, and other clinical data for longitudinal disease monitoring. The project will develop an integrated database incorporating clinical, imaging, pathological, molecular, and biospecimen data. It will characterize the relationships of baseline tissue multi-omics features and longitudinal changes in CSF- and blood-derived ctDNA/cfRNA with treatment response, recurrence prediction, and prognosis. The study will also develop diagnostic and risk-stratification models applicable to patients at our institution, across the region, and potentially throughout mainland China, while establishing standardized operating procedures for biospecimen collection and processing. This work is expected to provide high-quality evidence and a sustainable translational research platform for elucidating the biological heterogeneity of PCNSL, validating liquid-biopsy biomarkers, and optimizing precision follow-up strategies.

title: Study of Collection and Analysis of Clinical, Anamnestic, Functional, Biological Data Through the Support of Artificial Intelligence to Evaluate the Possibility of Defining a Digital Twin of the Lung (LUCE)
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] This research study aims to retrospectively and prospectively analyze the clinical, anamnestic, functional, biological data of patients who have performed or will perform non-contrast chest photon count CT. The use of contrast medium is evaluated by the physician. Main objective The study aims to understand how many people who undergo non-contrast photon-counting chest CT have: lung nodules, chest tumors, and other non-cancerous lung diseases. Secondary objectives * Analyze the data with the help of artificial intelligence to create a "digital twin" of the lung, that is, a virtual copy of the lung that allows you to study and simulate the behavior of the lung for research and analysis purposes, without directly intervening on the patient. * Follow any suspicious lung changes over time to understand how they change and whether they are linked to clinical, biological, or laboratory parameters. The enrollment phase will last 12 months and will begin with the approval of the study. At this stage, clinical data already present in the patient's medical record and data relating to the photon count CT examination will be collected. After the enrollment phase, the patient will be observed for a further total duration of 10 years: in particular, a follow-up visit will be arranged at two, five and ten years. More specifically, if there are no radiological elements that require scheduling a visit to the center, the patient will be contacted by telephone for a telematic update of the data. If, however, pulmonary alterations are identified during the study, the patient will be referred to the Reference Operating Unit, as per clinical practice, to continue with the most appropriate personalized diagnostic-therapeutic process. In these cases, the patient will be contacted by telephone and an appointment with the institution will be suggested.

title: Stimuli-responsive CRISPR-based genome editing delivery system for cancer treatment: A review of fundamentals and applications.
text: Cancer remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Conventional modalities, namely surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy, continue to face substantial limitations. The advent of gene therapy, particularly CRISPR-based genome editing, offers new opportunities to overcome these barriers. Nuclease systems such as CRISPR/Cas9 enable precise excision of mutant alleles and targeted insertion of exogenous sequences by harnessing endogenous DNA-repair pathways, achieving durable and accurate genomic modification; derivative tools including CRISPRi, base editing, and prime editing enable diverse forms of gene regulation or precise genome modification through transcriptional repression, base conversion, or related editing mechanisms. To enhance the efficiency, specificity, and spatiotemporal control of CRISPR editing in vivo, sophisticated delivery platforms have been engineered to respond to endogenous tumor-microenvironment cues (e.g., pH, redox potential, hypoxia, ATP, enzymes and microRNAs) or exogenous triggers (e.g., light, ultrasound and magnetic fields). Distinct from material-centric classification schemes, this review organizes these stimuli-responsive systems according to their pathological relevance to the tumor microenvironment (TME), establishing a conceptual framework that links specific TME aberrations with corresponding delivery paradigms. These stimuli-responsive systems represent a major innovation and markedly expand the therapeutic potential of genome editing in oncology. In this review, we summarize the mechanistic basis of CRISPR-based editing, delineate design principles and engineering strategies for stimuli-responsive delivery, and highlight recent advances, outstanding challenges, and future directions toward clinical translation. We aim to provide a concise reference to guide the rational design of gene-editing cancer therapeutics.

title: CRISPR interference-based gene silencing in insects: from functional genomics to prospective insect-pest management applications.
text: Insect-pests remain a major constraint to global agriculture, causing yield losses through direct feeding and transmission of phytopathogens. Chemical pesticides and transgenic crops expressing Bacillus thuringiensis toxins have shown initial success; however, their use is increasingly constrained by resistance, non-target effects, environmental contamination and regulatory restrictions. Although RNA interference (RNAi) presents a targeted and eco-friendly alternative, it is limited by species variability, rapid double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) degradation, inconsistent silencing and off-target effects. Nuclease-active Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) enables genetic editing, but its irreversible genome modifications raise ethical, ecological and regulatory concerns. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) offers a programmable approach for sequence-specific, reversible transcriptional suppression without inducing double-strand DNA breaks. Using catalytically inactive Cas9 (dead Cas9 or dCas9) -guided by single-guide RNA (sgRNA), CRISPRi inhibits transcription initiation or elongation while maintaining genomic integrity. Experimental studies in insect models, including disease-vector mosquitoes, have demonstrated effective suppression of coding and non-coding genes, supporting CRISPRi as a functional genomics tool. This review discusses CRISPRi mechanisms, applications, advantages and limitations in insects, comparing it with RNAi and CRISPR/Cas9. Overall, current evidences indicate that CRISPRi is a precise and non-mutagenic platform for insect-pest management, particularly where controlled, reversible and species-specific gene regulation is desirable. However, its application in agricultural pest management remains an extrapolation from functional-genomics studies and requires validation in pest species under whole-organism and field-relevant conditions.

title: Efficient Bioproduction of Citric Acid in Aspergillus niger.
text: Citric acid is the most widely produced organic acid in industrial biotechnology, with a global annual output exceeding 2 million tons and broad applications across the food, pharmaceutical, chemical, and environmental sectors. Despite more than a century of industrial development since the discovery of citric acid fermentation by Aspergillus niger in 1917, current production systems are approaching critical bottlenecks in strain performance, process efficiency, and environmental sustainability. Increasing evidence indicates that citrate overproduction is not governed by a single metabolic pathway but emerges as a multi-constraint-driven systems phenomenon involving coordinated regulation of metabolism, cellular physiology, and environmental conditions. Recent advances in systems biology and synthetic biology have enabled a paradigm shift from empirical optimization to rational and programmable biomanufacturing. The integration of multi-omics data with genome-scale metabolic models has substantially deepened the understanding of citrate overflow metabolism. In parallel, the development of CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing, dynamic gene regulation systems, and promoter engineering has enabled precise and multiplexed rewiring of metabolic networks. Targeted engineering strategies focusing on carbon uptake, mitochondrial metabolism, citrate transport, and morphology regulation have demonstrated that high-level production requires coordinated multi-layer optimization rather than single-gene modifications. At the process level, emerging strategies, including immobilized fermentation, in situ product recovery, and the utilization of alternative non-food feedstocks, are being increasingly integrated with engineered strains to enhance productivity and sustainability. These advances collectively point toward a transition from conventional fermentation to a multi-scale, integrated biomanufacturing framework. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent progress in citric acid biomanufacturing, covering the evolution of industrial A. niger strains, systems-level mechanisms of citrate accumulation, synthetic biology-enabled tool development, rational chassis engineering strategies, and process intensification approaches. Finally, we discuss future directions, including dynamic metabolic control, artificial intelligence-assisted design, and circular biorefinery systems, aiming to establish a fully integrated, intelligent, and sustainable paradigm for next-generation citric acid production.

title: Survival of the fittest tool: choosing between open and closed artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical science
text: Three years ago, this journal published the editorial Technological Darwinism , urging pharmaceutical scientists to adapt to artificial intelligence (AI) rather than resist it. Since then, the question has shifted from whether to use AI to which AI to use, under what circumstances, and with what evidence. This review addresses that question by mapping current AI tools across the five canonical stages of drug development, from discovery to post-market pharmacovigilance. It is a narrative review, not a systematic one, and it treats openness as a spectrum rather than a binary. It compares two broad categories: open systems free, often open source or open weight, inspectable, and locally deployable and closed systems, which are proprietary, commercial, and delivered as a service. The central conclusion is pragmatic. For routine laboratory, educational, and research tasks, capable open tools now exist for almost every application, including manuscript drafting, literature review, reference management, statistical analysis, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modelling, calibration and standard-curve fitting, chemical structure drawing and SMILES handling, image and figure generation, and prediction of physicochemical, ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity), formulation, and excipient compatibility properties. Free web services, however, may require confidential structures to be uploaded to a third party, so openness is distinguished here from private deployment, and independent head to head evidence against commercial tools is uneven. In contrast, integrated end to end drug discovery and validated regulatory workflows remain dominated by proprietary platforms. During the period covered by this review, the first generative AI-designed molecule targeting a generative AI-derived protein reported positive Phase IIa results and entered Phase III in July 2026; protein structure prediction was recognized with the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, shared by Hassabis, Jumper and Baker and became partly open; an autonomous frontier language model improved a longstanding medicinal chemistry reaction through thousands of wet-laboratory experiments; and regulatory agencies issued their first guidance on AI credibility. The review argues that the most enduring competency is not mastery of any single AI platform but the ability to select appropriate tools, critically validate their outputs, and document their credibility in proportion to the decisions they inform. Accordingly, open AI systems should be the default for routine, low-risk, and educational applications, whereas proprietary platforms currently retain advantages for integrated discovery and regulated development. Credibility is defined operationally, human oversight is treated as a condition of use, and the review states where comparative evidence is lacking.

title: A multi-scale cell-type resolved map of trans-regulatory architecture in the aging human brain
text: Mapping genetic effects on distal genes and regulatory programs is essential for understanding how genetic variation influences complex diseases; yet trans-QTL discovery remains limited by weak effect sizes, extensive multiple testing and poor reproducibility. Here, we introduce TransMap, a generalizable computational framework that combines multi-scale trans-QTL mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization to improve the discovery and interpretation of distal regulatory variants. Beyond individual trans-eGenes, TransMap constructs local co-regulatory program phenotypes that account for background expression variation to improve the detection of weak, coordinated distal genetic effects. Across a broad range of simulation settings, TransMap achieved 9.2-36.7% higher trans-QTL discovery power than existing methods while maintaining well-controlled type I error rates. We applied TransMap to bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles from the aging human brain in the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), further integrating proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic biomarker measurements (average N=476 donors). Genome-wide fine-mapping of TransMap single-gene and program-level QTL yielded variant annotations with 2.75-2.88x heritability enrichment across 57 complex diseases and traits (average N=307K), with complementary heritability information captured across regulatory scales. Multi-phenotype colocalization identified 49,532 trans-regulatory events supported by shared genetic signals with cis-eQTL or biomarker-QTL, including 1,825 candidate cis-trans-biomarker regulatory configurations. TransMap further revealed an asymmetric cross-cell-type regulatory architecture in which neuronal cis-regulatory signals preferentially associate with coordinated glial trans-regulatory responses, supported by co-culture experiments and spatial transcriptomics. Alzheimers disease (AD) GWAS-prioritized colocalization identified trans-regulatory associations in 115 AD-associated loci, including a KNOP1 cis-eQTL associated in trans with a microglial regulatory program containing MS4A4E, with additional support from statistical mediation analysis. TransMap provides a multi-scale, cell-type-resolved atlas of trans-regulatory variation and a generalizable framework for elucidating the regulatory architecture of complex diseases.

title: Microplastics (MPs)-associated chemical components are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression via genomic instability and spatial microenvironment remodeling: A study based on integrated multi-omics analysis.
text: Microplastics (MPs) and their toxic components (BPA, DBP, DEHP) pose global health threats, with the liver as primary target. The mechanisms by which MPs may contribute to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression and spatial microenvironment remodeling remain poorly understood. We employed an integrated multi-omics workflow combining bulk transcriptomics, WGCNA, ten machine learning algorithms combined into 101 candidate model combinations, single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics (ST), inferCNV, CytoTRACE, and molecular docking with 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. We identified 22 hub genes at the putative intersection of HCC dysregulation and documented toxicological targets of MP-associated chemicals (BPA, DBP, and DEHP), enriched in cell cycle and senescence. A 6-gene (AKR1C3, AURKA, CCNB1, EZH2, FABP5, ESR1) risk model (glmBoost + SVM) achieved high diagnostic accuracy (mean external AUC = 0.965; internal bootstrap validation of the six-gene logistic model: bias-corrected AUC = 0.987 (optimism = 0.005). Single-cell analysis revealed risk genes localized in HCC parenchymal and myeloid cells, putatively positively correlating with CNV burden and stemness, while ESR1 showed inverse correlation. ST suggested spatial expression gradients of AKR1C3 and FABP5 with increasing malignancy. Molecular docking of all six hub targets against BPA, DBP, and DEHP, followed by 100 ns MD simulations of the AKR1C3-ligand complexes-the biologically most relevant sub-network-suggested structurally stable binding, with RMSD fluctuations (0.13-0.5 nm), maintained hydrogen bonds, stable Rg and SASA, low RMSF, and favorable free energy landscapes, supporting the structural plausibility of protein-ligand interactions. This study provides a multidimensional, hypothesis-generating landscape of HCC progression associated with MP-associated chemical exposure at single-cell and spatial resolutions, with dynamic and energetic evidence supporting the structural plausibility of stable plasticizer-target binding, offering novel toxicological targets and mechanistic insights for environmental and clinical intervention.

title: Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma: Biology-Driven Disease Model.
text: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is a unique lymphoid neoplasm in which rare malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells orchestrate an extensive, spatially organized immune and inflammatory microenvironment that determines diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic sensitivity. This review summarizes recent advances in the biopathology, diagnosis, and prognostic stratification of classic Hodgkin lymphoma, with particular emphasis on the emerging molecular subtyping framework proposed by Aoki and colleagues, which is not yet clinically validated, and on the proposed concept of classic Hodgkin lymphoma as a systemic immunobiological disease. In this narrative review, we examined the literature on classic Hodgkin lymphoma biology, the tumor immune microenvironment, diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers, and molecular classification, prioritizing studies published through to mid-2026 and distinguishing established evidence from observational associations, preclinical findings, meeting abstracts, ongoing trials, and hypotheses, including single-cell, spatial, and liquid biopsy technologies, and integrating the authors' own recent work on immune and inflammatory biomarkers and on the systemic immunobiological features of classic Hodgkin lymphoma. Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells sustain disease through constitutive NF-κB and JAK/STAT signaling, 9p24.1-driven PD-L1/PD-L2 overexpression, and secretion of chemokines and cytokines that recruit and functionally reprogram CD4+ T cells, regulatory T cells, macrophages, and stromal cells. Multidimensional profiling integrating malignant-cell genomics, spatial transcriptomics, and imaging mass cytometry has led to the proposal of four molecular subtypes of classic Hodgkin lymphoma (CST, CN913, STB, and CN2P), each defined by distinct genomic drivers and immune architecture, a hypothesis-generating framework that awaits prospective validation. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma has been proposed to be a systemic immunobiological disorder, with circulating tumor DNA, thymus and activation-regulated chemokine (TARC/CCL17), and peripheral immune signatures associated with disease activity beyond the lymph node; these markers are promising but remain investigational. Diagnosis is evolving from morphology-based assessment toward precision immunopathology integrating spatial and digital pathology, while prognosis is progressively incorporating tissue-based, circulating, spatial, and molecular biomarkers into integrated risk models that are, for the most part, still investigational and are being tested in biomarker-directed clinical trials. The convergence of molecular subtyping, spatial immunobiology, systemic disease biology, and liquid biopsy may reshape the diagnostic and prognostic landscape of classic Hodgkin lymphoma, suggesting a potential transition from anatomically defined, morphology-based assessment toward integrated, biology-driven precision medicine. This transition has unfolded stepwise, from tissue-based immunophenotyping and spatial biomarkers, through circulating markers such as ctDNA and TARC/CCL17, to genomically defined molecular subtypes now being linked to systemic immune readouts and tested in biomarker-directed trials. Prospective validation, assay standardization, and evidence of clinical utility are required before these approaches can enter routine practice.

title: Identification of Key Fatty acid Metabolism-Related Genes in Vascular Dementia.
text: Vascular dementia (VaD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by chronic cerebral hypoperfusion and cognitive decline, yet the role of fatty acid metabolism in its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. Integrated transcriptomic profiling was combined with network-based analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and machine learning to uncover key fatty acid metabolism-associated molecular features associated with VaD. Single-cell RNA sequencing, intercellular communication inference, and in silico perturbation analyses were applied to define immune-stromal interactions. Potential therapeutic compounds were evaluated using molecular docking and dynamics simulations. We identified three VaD-related fatty acid metabolism genes (VaD-FAMRGs), namely PNPLA3, HSP90AA1, and ALB, which showed consistent diagnostic performance across multiple computational approaches and were associated with lipid metabolism, inflammatory processes, and neurovascular unit dysfunction. Functional enrichment, single-cell RNA sequencing, and in silico gene perturbation analyses provided exploratory insights into the potential associations of these candidate genes with lipid transport, metabolic regulation, synaptic maintenance, and immune-inflammatory processes. Cell-cell communication analysis further revealed activation of the ANGPTL signaling axis, suggesting impaired endothelial-glial interactions driven by lipid metabolic dysregulation. Regulatory network analysis identified key transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulators, including REST, miR-155-5p, and miR-21-5p, which may coordinately modulate VaD-FAMRG expression. Drug repurposing analysis highlighted quercetin as a candidate compound with predicted interactions with all three hub proteins, supported by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations. These findings suggest that dysregulated fatty acid metabolism may be associated with the development and progression of VaD through coordinated metabolic, inflammatory, and neurovascular mechanisms. This study provides a systems-level framework for understanding the underlying pathological processes and establishes a theoretical basis for future mechanistic and experimental validation.

title: Targeting Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases in Cancer: Dual Roles and Therapeutic Implications.
text: Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases (PTPs) play a dual role in cancer as both tumor suppressors and oncogenic drivers by dephosphorylating key signaling molecules. They take part in core oncogenic pathways, either suppressing tumor formation or promoting cancer progression through proliferation and immune suppression. Recent therapeutic advances have explored allosteric inhibitors, degraders and combination approaches targeting non-catalytic regulatory domains or the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Combined with immune checkpoint blockade, these strategies have potential to resolve selectivity limitations of traditional catalytic-site inhibitors alongside hard-to-target and dual-role challenges. This paper proposes a paradigm shift from single enzyme activity inhibition to microenvironment regulation and combination strategies, emphasizing the need to target non-catalytic regions and integrate the Tumor Microenvironment (TME) using single-cell spatial transcriptomics and biomarker analysis to advance combinations of PTP inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors from preclinical models toward early-phase clinical investigation. METHOD: We conducted a narrative review of PubMed through October 2026 and hand-searched reference lists of relevant guidelines, reviews, and primary studies. We prioritized international guidance, systematic reviews, multicenter registries, prospective cohorts, and clinically informative mechanistic studies. Case reports and experimental studies were kept when they addressed questions not covered by higher-level evidence. The review was not protocol driven and did not include duplicate screening, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or a PRISMA flow diagram.

title: Evolution of Automated Insulin Delivery Devices in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: A Narrative Review.
text: Insulin delivery has evolved through distinct technological phases, each improving the usability and dosing control and accuracy. This review traces the historical evolution of insulin delivery devices through distinct eras, beginning with the early use of insulin syringes for manual administration, followed by the introduction of insulin pens that improved portability and dosing precision. Subsequently, the emergence of continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII), sensor-augmented pump (SAP) therapy, and finally, the automated insulin delivery (AID) systems, have created a significant breakthrough in the evolution of modern diabetes care. Safety-oriented automation, including low-glucose suspend (LGS) and predictive low-glucose suspend (PLGS), marked the first steps toward closed-loop control. The commercialization of hybrid closed-loop (HCL) systems represented a paradigm shift, enabling real-time, algorithm-driven basal insulin modulation and significantly improving glycemic outcomes, including increased time in range (TIR) and reduced hypoglycemia. Advanced hybrid closed-loop (AHCL) systems have since introduced customizable targets, automated correction boluses, and interoperability standards, creating flexible ecosystems for personalized diabetes management. Fully closed-loop systems have entered clinical trials offering automated insulin delivery independent of meal announcements. Despite these advances, adoption remains limited by suboptimal user-friendliness, intensive training requirements, and high costs leading to inequitable access, with an ongoing need for user engagement, alarm management, and periodic troubleshooting in real-world settings. Looking ahead, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and neural network-based algorithms is expected to drive the next wave of innovation, enabling more adaptive, autonomous, and patient-centered diabetes care.

title: Securing Cell-Free Expression: Safeguards for Distributed Biomanufacturing.
text: Cell-free expression (CFE) is an acellular biomanufacturing platform capable of producing diverse biomolecules, including proteins, enzymes, and mRNA, outside of living cells. Unlike traditional bioproduction, which requires sterile culture systems and large-scale bioreactors, CFE enables rapid, modular, and decentralized synthesis. CFE extracts can be freeze-dried, stored for extended periods, and reactivated on demand by simply adding a nucleic acid template. This makes it particularly suited for point-of-need applications such as diagnostics, vaccines, and potentially therapeutics in remote, resource-limited, or emergency settings. However, the same features introduce novel biosecurity concerns. Commercially available CFE kits already support the production of bacteriophages and virus-like particles with minimal specialized equipment. As benchtop DNA synthesis and CFE technologies become increasingly accessible, barriers of skill, facilities, and resources are significantly reduced, enabling malicious actors or small autonomous groups to generate harmful biological agents. To address these risks while enabling safe deployment, we recommend: (1) investing in yield optimization and the development of modular, good manufacturing practice-compatible CFE units for distributed manufacturing (performance and scalability); (2) engineering CFE systems with bioorthogonal or otherwise nontransferable components to reduce potential misuse (intrinsic safety feature); and (3) implementing risk-based restrictions for different CFE formulations, balancing innovation with security oversight (tiered access controls). By combining these measures, CFE can be responsibly integrated into global health security infrastructure, delivering its transformative benefits without compromising biosecurity.

title: Emerging gene and stem cell therapies for hereditary hearing loss: from molecular correction to regenerative reconstruction.
text: Hearing loss is among the most common sensory impairments globally and remains a significant unmet clinical challenge. Current rehabilitative approaches, such as hearing aids and cochlear implants, provide partial functional compensation but fail to restore the structural and physiological integrity of the cochlea. This review summarizes progress in therapeutic development targeting key deafness-associated genes, including OTOF, GJB2, and SLC26A4, highlighting the rationale, current clinical evidence, and major translational challenges. We further discuss the potential of combining gene therapy with stem cell-based approaches to promote inner ear regeneration and restore sensorineural function. Emerging technologies such as CRISPR/Cas, adeno-associated virus, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived otic progenitors have opened new avenues for causal correction and tissue reconstruction. Integrated therapeutic models that combine gene or stem cell therapy with cochlear implants are reshaping the treatment paradigm from symptom management to biological repair. Advances in gene editing, gene delivery, and stem cell technologies are establishing these approaches as promising treatments for hereditary hearing loss, with ongoing progress expected to accelerate clinical translation despite remaining challenges in delivery efficiency, immune responses, ethics, and long-term efficacy. Collectively, these advances mark a pivotal step toward personalized and regenerative interventions for hereditary hearing loss.

title: Multicenter CT-Based Deep Learning for Preoperative Nodal Risk Stratification in Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma.
text: Accurate preoperative risk stratification for lymph node metastasis (LNM) in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) remains difficult. We developed and validated ThyLNT, a Transformer-based 2.5D deep learning model using preoperative computed tomography (CT), and explored related biological features in multi-omics analyses. A total of 1560 patients with PTC from six hospitals were retrospectively included. The Tongji Hospital cohort was divided into training and internal validation sets, and five external cohorts were used for independent testing. Seven 2.5D tumor slices were extracted per patient, encoded with a DenseNet201 backbone, and fused by a Transformer. Model performance was compared with radiomics, ensemble learning, and multi-instance learning using AUC, calibration, decision curve, and precision-recall analyses. Bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics were used to explore related biological features. ThyLNT achieved an AUC of 0.882 (CI, 0.858-0.905) in the training cohort, 0.787 (CI, 0.738-0.835) in the internal validation cohort, and 0.772 (CI, 0.662-0.878) to 0.827 (CI, 0.763-0.885) across the five external cohorts. It showed multicenter discrimination, whereas calibration and threshold-dependent operating characteristics varied across cohorts. Multi-omics analyses provided exploratory biological context, including candidate associations with vascular endothelial growth factor A-related signaling and lipid metabolism. ThyLNT demonstrated multicenter performance for preoperative LNM prediction in PTC and may support risk stratification, although calibration, threshold use, and clinical utility require prospective validation.

title: Engineered Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) as Carriers for CRISPR/Cas9 Therapeutics: Recent Advances in Cargo Loading and Targeted Delivery.
text: The therapeutic potential of CRISPR/Cas genome editing has advanced the development of precision medicine; however, its clinical translation for many in vivo applications remains limited by challenges in achieving safe, efficient, and targeted delivery. Conventional viral vectors and synthetic nanocarriers are associated with challenges including immunogenicity, limited cargo capacity, prolonged nuclease expression, off-target effects, and manufacturing complexities. Engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) are being investigated as alternative delivery carriers due to their biological origin, capacity for cargo encapsulation, and opportunities for surface functionalization. However, their biocompatibility, immunogenicity, and ability to cross biological barriers depend on vesicle source, formulation, and experimental conditions. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in the design of engineered EVs for CRISPR/Cas delivery, with a particular focus on strategies to improve cargo loading, targeting specificity, and therapeutic efficacy. We discuss the advantages and limitations of different CRISPR cargo formats, including plasmid DNA, mRNA, and ribonucleoprotein complexes, together with endogenous and exogenous loading approaches, hybrid EV platforms, and methods for enhancing intracellular delivery. Advances in EV surface engineering through genetic, chemical, physical, and biomimetic modifications are highlighted as strategies being investigated to improve tissue-specific delivery and functional cargo transport. The review also highlights emerging research directions, including CRISPR-EV theranostic platforms and the application of artificial intelligence to enhance CRISPR-EV therapeutic systems. Finally, key translational challenges, including scalable production, EV heterogeneity, cargo-loading efficiency, biodistribution, regulatory standardization, and quality control, are critically discussed. EV-mediated CRISPR delivery remains at an early preclinical stage, with clinical safety and therapeutic efficacy yet to be established. Further advances in EV engineering, cargo-loading strategies, and manufacturing standardization are needed to support its potential clinical translation.

title: Precision gene targeting: comparative roles of siRNA, miRNA, and CRISPR technologies in gene silencing and genome editing: a review.
text: Precision gene targeting has emerged as a powerful approach for selectively regulating gene expression and modifying disease-associated genetic pathways. Among the principal technologies, small interfering RNA (siRNA), microRNA (miRNA), CRISPR-Cas9, and CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) provide distinct yet complementary strategies for gene regulation and genome manipulation. siRNAs mediate sequence-specific post-transcriptional gene silencing through degradation of complementary messenger RNA, enabling potent and generally transient suppression of target genes. In contrast, miRNAs are endogenous regulatory RNAs that modulate multiple transcripts through translational repression and mRNA destabilization, thereby influencing diverse cellular processes and regulatory networks. CRISPR-Cas9 expands the scope of precision gene targeting by enabling programmable modification of genomic DNA, whereas CRISPRi uses catalytically inactive Cas9 to achieve targeted transcriptional repression without introducing DNA double-strand breaks. This review provides a comparative and critical analysis of these technologies, emphasizing their molecular mechanisms, target recognition, specificity, delivery strategies, therapeutic applications, clinical development, advantages, limitations, and safety considerations. Collectively, these platforms have demonstrated therapeutic potential across a broad range of diseases, including cancer, genetic and metabolic disorders, cardiovascular and neurological diseases, infectious diseases, and ocular disorders. However, important barriers to clinical translation remain, including delivery limitations, molecular stability, target and off-target effects, immunogenicity, toxicity, genomic instability, and the need for precise and durable control of gene modulation. For CRISPR-based approaches, additional considerations include modality-specific genomic alterations, prolonged editor activity, and the ethical and regulatory implications of permanent genome modification. Continued advances in molecular engineering, delivery technologies, target-selection strategies, and platform optimization may improve the specificity, safety, durability, and therapeutic efficacy of these approaches and facilitate their responsible integration into precision medicine.

title: TISCH3: an expanded resource for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of the tumor microenvironment.
text: The Tumor Immune Single Cell Hub (TISCH) is a curated resource for exploring single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from the tumor microenvironment. Here, we present TISCH3, which expands the single-cell collection from 190 to 408 datasets and introduces 69 spatial transcriptomics datasets, bringing the total to 477 datasets. The 218 newly added scRNA-seq datasets span 48 cancer types, and the spatial collection spans 27 cancer types. Spatial samples are curated and processed individually, and single-cell references enable estimation of cell-type composition at each spot. The spatial workspace comprises six modules: Overview, GeneExp, spatially variable genes (SVGs), CellAssoc, Communication, and Downloads. These modules provide sample metadata and quality-control views, spatial gene expression maps, ranking of SVG, cell-type correlation and conditional intra-spot co-occurrence analyses, inferred cell-cell communication networks, and downloadable data and results. TISCH3 retains the single-cell analysis capabilities of TISCH2 and extends them to spatial exploration of the tumor microenvironment. The database is freely available without registration at https://tisch3.compbio.cn/.

title: Navigating the Drought Tolerance-Yield Trade-Off in Triticeae Cereals: From Molecular Networks to Climate-Resilient Breeding.
text: Drought driven by climate change severely threatens food security, particularly for wheat and barley grown in water-limited regions. A major breeding challenge is the trade-off between drought tolerance and yield. This review synthesises current knowledge of drought adaptation mechanisms in Triticeae crops, focusing on the transcriptional cascades, ABA-centric hormonal signalling and posttranslational modifications (kinases, phosphatases and ubiquitination) that confer resilience while often constraining carbon allocation to developing grains. Recent genomic advances, including genome-wide association study (GWAS), multi-omics integration and single-cell RNA-transcriptomics, have uncovered a wealth of drought-associated loci, although their translational potential is limited by data heterogeneity, environmental dependency and a persistent gap between laboratory validation and field performance. Emerging breeding approaches, such as speed breeding, wild-allele introgression, multiplex CRISPR/Cas9 and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven phenotyping are accelerating the development of climate-smart cultivars. Tissue-specific and inducible expression systems show early promise in uncoupling stress protection from growth penalties. Looking ahead, we propose that overcoming the yield-tolerance trade-off will require integrating synthetic biology, explainable AI, systematic exploration of novel variation and field phenomics coupled with digital twin modelling. Collectively, this review provides a strategic framework for engineering next-generation, climate-smart Triticeae cereals capable of maintaining productivity under intensifying drought conditions.

title: A safety-constrained AI framework for CAR-T design in solid tumors
text: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematological malignancies, but its translation to solid tumors remains limited by antigen heterogeneity, poor tumor infiltration, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments, and on-target/off-tumor toxicity. Here, we present a safety-constrained artificial intelligence framework for rational CAR-T design in solid tumors. The workflow integrates four linked stages: CD-antigen prioritization, safety-by-design CAR architecture mapping, constrained large language model (LLM)–assisted reasoning, and statistical feature-structure analysis. Curated CD-antigen functional annotations and tumor-associated expression descriptors were encoded into a multi-criteria scoring system that stratified targets into high-confidence, conditional, and unsafe classes. Across the analyzed CD-antigen space, 38% of markers were classified as high-confidence candidates, 34% as conditional targets requiring logic-gated or controllable architectures, and 28% as unsafe targets because of predicted off-tumor risk. External benchmark analysis using MSLN, HER2/ERBB2, EGFR/EGFRvIII, CEA/CEACAM5, GD2, B7-H3/CD276, and CD47 supported the framework’s ability to distinguish direct targets from safety-constrained or unsuitable candidates. An updated four-model LLM benchmark, including GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.5, Grok 4.5, and Claude Sonnet 5, showed convergence toward dual-antigen logic-gated, trafficking-enhanced, and armored CAR designs, while revealing model-dependent differences in safety awareness, traceability, and hallucination risk. Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol showed the strongest safety-oriented performance, whereas Grok 4.5 required greater expert oversight. Correlation and clustering analyses further identified redundant safety-liability features and candidate antigen combinations for logic-gated CAR design. This study provides a reproducible, human-in-the-loop decision-support framework for generating safety-aware CAR-T hypotheses. The framework is computational and hypothesis-generating and does not constitute experimental validation of CAR-T efficacy or safety.

title: High-Throughput Technologies for Targeted Covalent Drug Discovery: Recent Advances and Perspectives.
text: Covalent drugs have attracted increasing attention in modern drug discovery because of their prolonged target engagement, enhanced pharmacological efficacy, and potential to address traditionally challenging protein targets. The rapid development of electrophilic warhead chemistry, chemical biology methods, and high-throughput screening technologies has shifted covalent drug discovery from serendipitous identification to target-oriented and rational design. In recent years, phage display, mRNA display, and DNA-encoded library technologies have enabled the efficient de novo discovery of covalent peptides and small molecules, expanding the accessible chemical space for targeting cysteine, lysine, tyrosine, serine, and other reactive residues. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence has further accelerated covalent drug research by supporting covalent database construction, binding-site prediction, virtual screening, molecular generation, and structure-based ligand optimization. This article reviews recent advances in high-throughput strategies for targeted covalent drug discovery, with a focus on phage display, mRNA display, DNA-encoded libraries, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches. We further discuss current challenges and future opportunities in the field and provide our perspectives on emerging directions for next-generation covalent ligand discovery.

title: Artificial intelligence-guided open-source CRISPR tools for designer crops.
text: AI-guided protein design enables rational optimization of clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR) components. Das et al. harnessed the AI-designed OpenCRISPR-1 to create a suite of tools for plant gene editing. Their open-source platform, PlantOpenCRISPR-1, targets academic and translational use and could offer a more accessible option for researchers facing licensing barriers, highlighting open-source CRISPR's future potential.

title: Gene Therapy for Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type I: Current Advances, Clinical Translation, and Future Perspectives.
text: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD) is a group of rare autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiencies characterized by impaired leukocyte migration resulting from defective expression or function of adhesion molecules. The most common and severe form, LAD-I, is caused by biallelic mutations in Integrin Subunit Beta 2 (ITGB2), which encodes the β2-integrin subunit CD18, leading to recurrent life-threatening infections and impaired wound healing. LAD-II arises from mutations in the fucose-metabolism gene SLC35C1, and LAD-III from mutations in FERMT3, which disrupt integrin activation through kindlin-3. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has historically been the only established curative treatment for severe LAD-I, but donor availability, conditioning toxicity, and graft-versus-host disease limit its use and have motivated the development of autologous approaches. Autologous gene therapy using self-inactivating lentiviral vectors to introduce functional ITGB2 into patient-derived hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells has shown promising clinical results, including restored CD18 expression, improved leukocyte function, and fewer severe infections. In March 2026, the FDA granted accelerated approval to marnetegragene autotemcel (Kresladi; RP-L201), making it the first approved gene therapy for severe LAD-I in the United States. CRISPR/Cas9, base editing, and prime editing are also being investigated as alternative approaches for correcting ITGB2 mutations, although their application in LAD-I remains preclinical. These methods could allow correction of pathogenic ITGB2 variants without relying on integrating viral vectors, but their efficacy and long-term safety in LAD-I have yet to be established. However, conditioning-related toxicity, the need for long-term safety monitoring, and the complexity and cost of manufacturing remain important limitations to wider clinical use. This review examines the molecular basis of LAD, preclinical and clinical studies of gene therapy for LAD-I, and the challenges that remain in translating genome-editing approaches into clinical practice.

title: Network toxicology and single-cell transcriptomics identify acrylamide- and glycidamide-related candidate biomarkers in diabetic ulcers.
text: Diabetic ulcers (DU) are severe complications of diabetes, and environmental contaminants such as acrylamide (AA) and its metabolite glycidamide (GA) have been associated with metabolic disturbances relevant to diabetes. In this study, public transcriptomic datasets, network toxicology, protein interaction analysis, and machine learning were integrated to identify plausible candidate DU-associated biomarkers overlapping with predicted AA or GA targets. Functional enrichment, immune infiltration analysis, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and single-cell RNA sequencing were further applied to characterize their biological roles and cellular distribution. Eight candidate genes were identified from the intersection of differentially expressed genes and predicted toxicant targets, and PNP and CTSB were ultimately identified as plausible candidate DU-associated biomarkers. These genes were associated with proteasome function, DNA damage and repair, immune dysregulation, and altered cell communication. Single-cell analysis highlighted macrophages and T cells as major cell populations with dynamic plausible candidate biomarker expression. ELISA in streptozotocin induced diabetic ulcer mice further confirmed significantly increased CTSB and PNP protein levels, providing preliminary protein-level support for their association with DU. However, the overlap of PNP and CTSB with predicted AA/GA targets represents hypothesis-generating computational evidence only and does not establish that AA/GA exposure modulates these genes in vivo. These findings support PNP and CTSB as plausible candidate DU-associated biomarkers, while the predicted AA/GA-related associations require direct exposure-based experimental validation.

title: An SPP1-Associated Macrophage State Marks Lesion-Centred Inflammatory Persistence During Subacute Spinal Cord Injury.
text: Persistent subacute neuroinflammation limits tissue repair after spinal cord injury (SCI), yet how macrophage state heterogeneity is organized within lesion-centered inflammatory niches remains unclear. We integrated time-resolved mouse single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics with trajectory analysis, regulatory network inference, ligand activity analysis, exploratory in silico Spp1 perturbation, and interpretable machine learning, followed by tissue-level and donor-recipient validation. Time-resolved profiling revealed early neutrophil and monocyte recruitment, subsequent macrophage accumulation, and delayed microglial activation. Macrophage subclustering resolved seven injury-responsive states comprising inflammatory, transitional, tissue-associated, lipid-associated, SPP1-associated, repair-associated, and homeostatic programs. Among these states, SPP1_Mac expanded prominently, peaked at 7 days post-injury, and retained marked inflammatory activity. Spatial mapping localized the SPP1_Mac signature and focal Spp1 expression to lesion-centered regions within a broader Cd44-enriched cellular territory. Regulatory network, ligand activity, communication, and machine learning analyses prioritized SPP1-associated signaling within this state-niche organization. Injured spinal cords showed increased lesion-associated SPP1 and CD44 expression and enrichment of SPP1 within IBA1-positive myeloid regions. In a BV2-to-RAW264.7 donor-recipient system, donor cell Spp1 silencing attenuated recipient cell CD44 and CD86 expression, the proportion of F4/80⁺CD86⁺ cells, and IL-1β and TNF-α secretion following conditioned medium transfer. Together, these findings support a state-niche-communication framework in which SPP1_Mac represents a prominent cellular feature associated with lesion-centered inflammatory persistence during subacute SCI, providing a biological foundation for further stage-informed investigation of the post-SCI inflammatory microenvironment.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 editing of myeloid lectins reveals target-dependent transcriptional remodeling in tumor-associated macrophages.
text: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) integrate multiple microenvironmental signals, including lectin-mediated recognition of tumor-associated glycans. Although several myeloid lectins have been implicated in tumor-macrophage interactions, their contributions to immunosuppressive TAM phenotypes remain poorly defined. We implemented a CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) workflow in primary human monocytes to enable comparative loss-of-function interrogation of five potentially immunosuppressive lectins we previously reported. CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery conditions were benchmarked in freshly isolated monocytes using CD14 as a technical target, followed by sgRNA editing efficiency screening for CLEC4E, CLEC6A, CD209, SELL, and SIGLEC9 in HeLa S3 cells. Selected guides were applied to primary monocytes before co-culture in a 3D model with BT474 breast cancer cells. Editing was quantified by Sanger-sequencing deconvolution, while co-culture-derived CD45+ macrophages were isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting and characterized by bulk RNA sequencing. All five lectins were successfully perturbed, although gene editing efficiency remained target- and donor-dependent. Transcriptomic analysis revealed target-specific reprogramming and recurrent immunometabolic responses. mTORC1 signaling was consistently enriched, together with the remodeling of cholesterol homeostasis, fatty acid metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation. CLEC6A deletion achieved attenuation of hypoxia-, angiogenesis-, and TNF/NF-κB-associated programs. CD209 and SIGLEC9 deletion similarly reduced hypoxia- and angiogenesis-associated signatures while promoting lipid and oxidative metabolism. CLEC4E perturbation induced broad remodeling of lipid and oxidative metabolism and stress-response, despite comparatively limited editing efficiency. Comparative lectin perturbation thus identified CLEC6A as the strongest candidate for further mechanistic investigation, while CLEC4E showed broad transcriptional remodeling despite lower editing efficiency, supporting its prioritization for improved genetic interrogation. Responses to CD209 and SIGLEC9 targeting further support tumor glycan-myeloid signaling as a regulator of TAM state. Overall, lectin perturbation redirected TAM transcriptional states through distinct immunometabolic programs rather than a uniform pro-inflammatory polarization, highlighting lectin-dependent immunometabolic regulation as a promising axis for further investigation.

title: Systematic clustering alignment and feature characterization for single-cell omics using ACE-OF-Clust.
text: Clustering is widely used to identify cell types in cellular-resolution transcriptomic data, including single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST). Mixed-membership clustering assigns fractional memberships across clusters and captures continuous variation beyond hard clustering, but integrating and interpreting results from either approach is complicated by the "clustering alignment problem," which arises from label switching, multi-modality, and differences in model settings (including differing numbers of clusters). We introduce ACE-OF-Clust, enabling a four-step workflow for single-cell clustering: multiple clustering, clustering alignment, model comparison, and identification of informative features. ACE-OF-Clust introduces direct comparison of clustering solutions, assesses consistency against annotations, and leverages feature-level clustering profiles to prioritize genes discriminating among cell types, as well as to evaluate how gene sets contribute to clustering patterns. We demonstrate its utility using PBMC scRNA-seq data, breast cancer and mouse embryo ST data, and single-cell multi-omic data. ACE-OF-Clust quantifies cross-omic clustering variability and suggests putative cross-omic regulatory links. Overall, ACE-OF-Clust increases the interpretability, flexibility, and robustness of single-cell clustering, providing a scalable tool for studying cellular heterogeneity and gene expression dynamics.

title: Differential scanning calorimetry and artificial intelligence for analytical profiling of disease-related plasma thermograms.
text: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) is a systems-level thermodynamic tool for probing disease-related changes in complex biological fluids, yet clinical translation is hindered by challenges in thermogram interpretation, reproducibility, and data integration. DSC captures heat capacity transitions from multistate protein unfolding, reflecting collective stability landscapes of the plasma proteome. Pathological conditions can induce reproducible thermogram distortions, suggesting their utility as ensemble biomarkers beyond conventional scalar descriptors. Recent advances in ultrasensitive and microfluidic DSC have improved stability and reduced sample needs, while artificial intelligence enables extraction of distributed calorimetric features beyond melting temperature and enthalpy. Machine learning strategies-including statistical, kernel-based, deep learning, and physics-informed frameworks-help identify informative thermodynamic patterns. This review integrates thermodynamic principles, data-driven analytics, and clinical studies to assess DSC's capabilities and limitations. We further propose practical standardization and minimum-reporting frameworks for DSC acquisition, preprocessing, AI model development, and validation to improve reproducibility and cross-study comparability. Persistent issues such as inter-laboratory variability, cohort heterogeneity, small datasets, and regulatory hurdles continue to restrict routine use. Overall, combining DSC with AI offers a promising analytical framework for extracting clinically meaningful thermodynamic insights and advancing disease characterization.

title: Tumor-Specific Gene Editing Enhances Cancer Immunogenicity through Succinate Metabolism-Mediated MHC-I Reprogramming.
text: Impaired expression of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) greatly compromises cytotoxic T-cell-mediated anticancer immunotherapy. Existing MHC-I activation strategies are greatly challenged by poor tumor specificity and off-target toxicity. Herein, we report a dual tumor-specific CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system that can precisely knock out succinate dehydrogenase subunit C (Sdhc) to activate the MHC-I pathway via epigenetic and transcriptional regulation. A tumor-specific gene editor is first engineered via reversible shielding of sgRNA using an apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1)-responsive, complementary ssDNA, yielding AP-sgRNA with blocked editing activity in normal cells yet completely restored activity in APE1-overexpressing tumor cells. Subsequently, tumor-targeted delivery of AP-sgRNA and Cas9 mRNA (mCas9) is achieved using dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated lipid nanoparticle (DLNP), which upon bioorthogonal click reaction can anchor cancer cells that are prelabeled with azido groups using the unnatural sugar DCL-AAM. Thus, AP-sgSdhc/mCas9@DLNP enables efficient and selective Sdhc editing in tumor cells, leading to epigenetic and transcriptional activation of MHC-antigen processing and presentation genes and thereby provoking robust antitumor efficacy in the B16-OVA melanoma model through enhanced, T cell-mediated immune responses. Moreover, it completely suppressed pulmonary metastasis after combination with aPD-L1 in the 4T1 lung metastasis model. This study provides an enlightened paradigm for precision gene editing and renders a promising mechanism for potentiating cancer immunotherapy.

title: Spatial Multi-Omics Integration with Mass Spectrometry Imaging: Decoding Metabolic Landscapes and Disease Mechanisms.
text: Spatial multi-omics links molecular measurements to tissue architecture, but integrating spatial transcriptomics with mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) remains challenging because the modalities differ in sampling unit, spatial resolution, data structure, and molecular-identification certainty. This review synthesizes the enabling technologies and presents an evidence-calibrated workflow spanning tissue acquisition, spatial registration, modality-specific preprocessing, cross-modal annotation, mechanistic modeling, and orthogonal validation. We examine how MSI can complement single-cell and spatial transcriptomic or proteomic measurements in studies of tumor-host interfaces, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, adipose-tissue organization, and decidualization at the maternal-fetal interface. Across these applications, spatial colocalization is most informative when annotation confidence is reported and key chemical identities are validated, registration error is quantified, and candidate cell-metabolite relationships are tested by isotope tracing or perturbation. We further discuss molecular ambiguity, resolution-sensitivity-throughput trade-offs, 3-dimensional reconstruction, interlaboratory reproducibility, and requirements for clinical translation. The central conclusion is that spatial multi-omics is best used to formulate anatomically explicit, falsifiable hypotheses rather than to infer causality from aligned maps alone.

title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia
text: SUMMARY The basal ganglia play essential roles in motor control, emotion, learning and reward processing. Their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, the gene regulatory programs defining basal ganglia cell-type identity and function remain poorly understood, limiting interpretation of disease-associated non-coding variants. Here, we present the first single-cell multiome atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical adult human donors. Joint profiling reveals cell-type-specific deployment of active and repressive cis -regulatory elements and gene regulatory networks, and suggests a combinatorial homeobox transcription factor code underlying cell identity. Integration with matched spatial transcriptomic MERFISH data uncovers regional heterogeneity of epigenomic landscapes. Comparative analysis between human and mouse medium spiny neurons uncovers conservation of core gene regulatory features. This atlas interprets non-coding risk variants of neuropsychiatric disorders and supports the development of a deep learning model to predict gene regulation and functional effects of disease-associated variants. HIGHLIGHTS Joint single-cell profiling of transcriptomes and three histone modifications across eight human basal ganglia regions characterizes active and repressive chromatin states at cell-type resolution. Cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs decode combinatorial homeobox TF grammar governing the identity and diversification of basal ganglia neurons. Intergrative analyses link noncoding neuropsychiatric risk variants to specific cell types, regulatory elements, and candidate target genes. A sequence-to-function deep-learning model predicts gene regulation from DNA sequence and prioritizes functional disease-associated variants.

title: OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics
text: Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

title: MASLD-Mitochondrial Digital Twin: Mapping mitonuclear epistasis to predict disease trajectory and systemic bioenergetic homeostasis
text: Abstract Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent chronic disorder with marked clinical heterogeneity and divergent outcomes. Current pathophysiological models fail to fully account for inter-individual variation in progression toward steatohepatitis and systemic multimorbidity. This Perspective posits the mitochondrion as an integrative functional hub where genomic predisposition, epigenomic plasticity, and bioenergetic signaling converge to shape the disease's longitudinal trajectory. We synthesize evidence from the mitonuclear interactome—the co-evolutionary and functional coordination between nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, hepatic epigenomic remodeling, and circulating mitochondrial metabotypes to propose a unified systems biology framework: the MASLD-Mitochondrial Digital Twin (MASLD-MDT). This multiscale platform integrates high-resolution biological data—including single-cell mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy, NAD+ redox dynamics, and the systemic efflux of mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs)—to simulate individualized disease kinetics. By reframing MASLD as a systemic mitochondriopathy, the MASLD-MDT could quantify critical bioenergetic thresholds, providing a novel metric for risk stratification and the in silico optimization of therapeutic deployment. This hypothesis-oriented instrument aims to advance the field toward a mitochondrial precision medicine strategy, enabling the discovery of targeted interventions to intercept multi-organ compromise.

title: Cognitive digital twins: A state-of-the-art review
text: Digital twins are a key enabling technology for Industry 4.0/5.0 that provide digital representations of physical systems for monitoring and decision-making support. However, the increasing complexity, autonomy, and connectivity of modern industrial systems challenge traditional digital twin approaches focused on simple replication. Therefore, advanced capabilities that go beyond mirroring physical assets are required to enable simulation, optimization, prediction, and adaptive behavior. Cognitive digital twins extend the capabilities of traditional digital twins by integrating cognitive functions such as perception, attention, memory, reasoning, problem-solving, and learning through artificial intelligence techniques, including machine learning. This review considers the differences between cognitive and traditional digital twins, and investigates the operationalization of cognitive functions. It examines how algorithms, software, tools, and frameworks are implemented for cognitive digital twins through a systematic literature review conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology. Moreover, it identifies current advancements; maps cognitive functions to applications; highlights underrepresented functions and implementation gaps in interoperability, validation, and learning infrastructure; and establishes opportunities for standardized evaluation and modular cross-sector designs.
